Is the idea that lawyers are more selfish than other people—brewers, or soap boilers, or bankers? I doubt it. They are just the average, and include good and bad like any other class. Judge Jeffreys was a monster; but, on the other hand, it was the lawyers of the seventeenth century who largely saved the liberties of this country. I doubt whether the world has ever produced a wiser, more unselfish, more heroic figure than Lincoln. And he was a lawyer. I doubt whether any man in politics to-day has made such financial sacrifices as Mr. Asquith has made. He had a practice at the Bar which, I believe, brought him in £10,000 a year, and had he devoted himself to it instead of to politics, would have brought him in far more, and he gave it up for a job immeasurably more burdensome that has never brought him more than £5000. He might have been Lord Chancellor, with a comfortable seat on the Woolsack and £10,000 a year, and he chose instead to sit in the House of Commons every day to be the target of every disappointed placeman. Ah, you say, but look at the glory. Well, look at it. I would, as Danton said, rather keep sheep on the hillside than meddle with the government of men. It is the most ungrateful calling on earth. And, whatever other defects may be attributed to Mr. Asquith, a passion for such an empty thing as glory is not one of them. You will discover more passion for glory in Mr. Churchill in five minutes than you will discover in Mr. Asquith in five years. And Mr. Churchill is not a lawyer.

message.content: The notion that lawyers are inherently more self-serving than individuals in other professions—like brewers, soap makers, or bankers—is one I find questionable. They represent a microcosm of society, encompassing both commendable and reprehensible individuals, just like any other group. Take Judge Jeffreys, for instance; he was undoubtedly a villain. Conversely, it was the legal professionals of the seventeenth century who played a significant role in safeguarding the freedoms of this nation. Few figures in history can rival the wisdom, selflessness, and heroism of Lincoln, who was also a lawyer. Likewise, in contemporary politics, few have made financial sacrifices comparable to those made by Mr. Asquith. His legal practice at the Bar reportedly generated an income of £10,000 annually, and had he chosen to focus solely on it rather than enter politics, he likely would have earned even more. Instead, he opted for a far more demanding role that never afforded him more than £5,000. Asquith could have risen to the position of Lord Chancellor, enjoying a prestigious lifestyle with a £10,000 salary, yet he decided to endure the trials of the House of Commons, becoming a target for every disappointed aspirant. One might argue, "But think of the glory!" To which I respond, as Danton famously remarked, I would prefer tending sheep in the hills to engaging in the governance of people. Politics is arguably the most thankless profession one can pursue. While Mr. Asquith may have his flaws, an obsession with the superficial allure of fame is certainly not among them. In just five minutes, you could observe more ambition for fame in Mr. Churchill than you would find in Mr. Asquith over five years, and interestingly, Churchill is not a lawyer.
